questions.question: Which condition makes the metrics $d_p$ and $d_q$ on $\boldsymbol{X}$ strongly equivalent?
options: For all $\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}$ there are $a,b>0$ with $a\,d_p(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})\le d_q(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})\le b\,d_p(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})$.
There are $a,b>0$ and $\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}$ with $a\,d_p(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})\le d_q(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})\le b\,d_p(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})$.
There are $a,b>0$ such that $a\,d_p(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})\le d_q(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})\le b\,d_p(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})$ for all $\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}$.
For all $a,b>0$ there are $\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}$ with $a\,d_p(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})\le d_q(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})\le b\,d_p(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})$.

questions.question: Suppose $a d_p\leq d_q\leq b d_p$ and $c d_q\leq d_r\leq e d_q$ for positive constants. Which constants can bound $d_r$ in terms of $d_p$?
options: $ac$ and $be$
$a+c$ and $b+e$
$a/e$ and $b/c$
$0$ and $1$ only

questions.question: What inequality defines strong equivalence of metrics $d_p$ and $d_q$?
options: $a d_p(x,y)\le d_q(x,y)\le b d_p(x,y)$ for some $a,b \ge 0$
$a d_p(x,y)\le d_q(x,y)\le b d_p(x,y)$ for some $a,b \gt 0$
$d_q(x,y)\le b\, d_p(x,y)$ for all $x,y$, for some $b \gt 0$
$a d_p(x,y)\le d_q(x,y)\le b d_p(x,y)$, $a,b>0$ depending on $x,y$

questions.question: On $\mathbb{R}^2$ the taxicab metric $d_1$ and the Euclidean metric $d_2$ satisfy $d_2(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})\le d_1(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})\le\sqrt{2}\,d_2(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})$ for all $\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}$. Which constants $a,b$ show $d_1\approx d_2$ in the form $a\,d_1\le d_2\le b\,d_1$?
Two metrics $d$ and $d'$ on a set $X$ have exactly the same convergent sequences, with the same limits. Does it follow that $d\approx d'$?
options: No: on $(-\pi/2,\pi/2)$ the metrics $|\tan x-\tan y|$ and $|x-y|$ share their convergent sequences, yet their ratio is unbounded.
Yes: inducing the same notion of convergence is what strong equivalence means.
Yes: strongly equivalent metrics have the same convergent sequences, and strong equivalence is an equivalence relation.
No: the same convergent sequences give only the upper bound $d'\le b\,d$, never the lower one.

questions.question: Let $a\,d_p\le d_q\le b\,d_p$ on $X$ with $a,b>0$, and let $x_k\to x$ under $d_p$, i.e. $d_p(x_k,x)\to0$. Why does $x_k\to x$ under $d_q$ as well?
options: Because $d_q(x_k,x)\le b\,d_p(x_k,x)$ and the right-hand side tends to $0$.
Because $a\,d_p(x_k,x)\le d_q(x_k,x)$ and the left-hand side tends to $0$.
Because strongly equivalent metrics give the same distance between any two points.
Because $d_p$ and $d_q$ are both metrics on the same set $X$, and convergence does not depend on the metric.

questions.question: On $\mathbb{R}^n$, why is the discrete metric $d_{\mathrm{disc}}$ not strongly equivalent to the Euclidean metric $d_2$?
options: For $\boldsymbol{x}\ne\boldsymbol{y}$, $d_{\mathrm{disc}}(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})=1$ while $d_2(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})$ can be arbitrarily small or arbitrarily large, so no fixed constants bound the ratio.
Because $d_{\mathrm{disc}}$ takes only the values $0$ and $1$, it is not a metric on $\mathbb{R}^n$.
Because the two metrics never agree on a pair of distinct points, so the inequality fails at every pair.
Because $d_2\le b\,d_{\mathrm{disc}}$ fails for far-apart points, while $a\,d_{\mathrm{disc}}\le d_2$ holds for a suitable $a>0$.
